extracted.intended_audience: comedians, comedy writers, performers, and analysts classifying or studying comedic styles
extracted.subtask_description: Classify or tag live/performance comedic material by its dominant and secondary subgenres, and evaluate how genre conventions are used or subverted relative to audience expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observational
rubrics_metrics.description: Draws attention to unnoticed humor in everyday life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common subjects: relationships, eating, travel, mundane situations. Signature phrasing/example: 'Did you ever notice…?' Focus is on revealing the comic strangeness of the ordinary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-Deprecating
rubrics_metrics.description: Performers target themselves and their foibles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comedian makes themselves the butt of the joke. Examples cited: Rodney Dangerfield, Larry David. Useful when building rapport or appearing humble; can risk undermining authority if overused.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anecdotal
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic personal stories (true or partly true, embellished).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes storytelling focus with long-form narrative beats rather than short quips. Expect setup, escalation, and payoff across multiple beats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blue (Off-Color / Risqué)
rubrics_metrics.description: Relies on impropriety / indecency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Topics often include sex, body, and taboo content. Tone can be explicit; appropriateness depends heavily on audience and context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dark / Black
rubrics_metrics.description: Morbid subjects such as war, death, crime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comedy emerges from the incongruity of pairing comedic tone with morbid or disturbing subject matter. Requires sensitivity to audience and context; can be provocative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wordplay
rubrics_metrics.description: Puns, double entendre, rhyme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surface-level linguistic techniques drive the humor (puns, clever phrasing, ambiguity). Often relies on language dexterity and timing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insult / Roast
rubrics_metrics.description: Targets others or self with direct insults.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typically requires a 'friendly contract' (mutual consent/understanding) when directed at individuals to avoid genuine offense. Can be used to establish hierarchy or affectionate ribbing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surreal / Absurdist
rubrics_metrics.description: Defies logic deliberately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses absurdity and reductio ad absurdum to create humor. Expectations of coherence are subverted; often non sequitur or dreamlike imagery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvisational
rubrics_metrics.description: Spontaneous, unscripted performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relies on 'yes-and' engine and performer responsiveness. Strengths include interactivity and freshness; risks include uneven payoff if performers miss beats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Slapstick / Physical
rubrics_metrics.description: Body-based humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Visual gags, pratfalls, exaggerated physicality. Best conveyed in visual/physical mediums rather than audio-only formats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topical / Political
rubrics_metrics.description: Draws on current events and politics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timeliness is crucial; references should be recognizably current. Can date material quickly but can also garner strong audience connection when timely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character-Based
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedian performs as a persona or character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus is on sustained persona traits and viewpoints. Examples: Andy Kaufman, Maria Bamford. Useful for exploring perspectives distinct from the performer’s real-life voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop Comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Uses objects as joke devices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physical props become the basis of jokes; examples include Carrot Top and Gallagher. Success depends on inventive prop design and staging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satire
rubrics_metrics.description: Critiques institutions or society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses humor to expose, mock, or criticize societal structures and practices. Examples: The Onion, The Daily Show. Often requires clarity of target and some level of audience knowledge about the subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre Mixing / Multiple Genres
rubrics_metrics.description: Most comedians mix multiple genres in their act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider that dominant and secondary genres can coexist; classification should allow for blended styles and hybrid approaches rather than forcing a single-label assignment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dominant subgenre identification
rubrics_metrics.description: What is the dominant subgenre?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine which single subgenre most strongly defines the performance or material. Look at overall tone, techniques used, recurring subjects, and performer persona to decide dominance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary genre identification
rubrics_metrics.description: What secondary genres mix in?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify additional subgenres that are present but not primary. Note how they complement or contrast with the dominant genre (e.g., observational with wordplay).

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience fit
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the genre fit the audience expectations?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the chosen genre(s) match the audience’s sensibilities, demographics, and context (e.g., blue humor with a conservative crowd may misfire). Consider venue and cultural norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use or subversion of conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Are genre conventions used or subverted?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the performer adheres to typical genre conventions (reinforcing expectations) or deliberately subverts them for effect. Note examples of common conventions and their manipulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedian reputation for genre
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the comedian known for this genre?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the performer’s broader body of work and public persona—are they recognized for this subgenre historically? Reputation affects audience framing and expectations.
